rows.stem: Which of the following ligands can show linkage isomerism in a coordination compound ?
rows.solution:
The NITRITE ion, \(\mathrm{NO_2^-}\), can show linkage isomerism.

Linkage isomerism requires an AMBIDENTATE ligand — one with two DIFFERENT donor atoms, of which it uses one at a time. The nitrite ion has both a nitrogen and two oxygens with lone pairs available, so it may attach through NITROGEN, giving the nitro form, or through an OXYGEN, giving the nitrito form. The two are genuinely different compounds, differing in colour and in stability.

Ammonia can donate only through its single nitrogen, so it has no choice to make. The oxalate ion has several oxygens but they are all the same KIND of donor atom, and it uses two of them AT ONCE — that makes it bidentate, not ambidentate, which is a different property altogether. The sulphate ion is likewise a one-kind donor.

The distinction to hold is between having a CHOICE of two different atoms and USING two atoms at the same time.

rows.stem: On adding \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution to 1 mole of complex \(\mathrm{NiCl_2 \cdot 4NH_3}\), two moles of AgCl are formed. The secondary valency of Ni in the complex will be :
rows.solution:
The secondary valency is FOUR.

Silver nitrate precipitates only the chloride that is FREE IN SOLUTION, outside the coordination sphere. Two moles of silver chloride from one mole of complex means BOTH chlorides are outside, acting as counter ions — so neither is a ligand.

The formula is therefore \(\mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_4]Cl_2}\): only the four ammonia molecules are inside the brackets.

Secondary valency is Werner's term for the COORDINATION NUMBER, the count of donor atoms bonded directly to the metal. Four ammonia molecules, each monodentate, give four.

The primary valency here is 2 — the two ionisable chlorides — and it corresponds to nickel's \(+2\) oxidation state. The question is careful to ask for the secondary one.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Transition elements form alloys easily because they have :
rows.solution:
Transition elements form alloys easily because they have NEARLY THE SAME ATOMIC SIZE.

An alloy is formed when atoms of one metal replace atoms of another in its crystal lattice. That substitution only works smoothly if the two kinds of atom are of comparable SIZE — a much larger or much smaller atom distorts the lattice and will not be accommodated.

Across a transition series the atomic radii change very little, because each added electron enters an inner \((n-1)d\) orbital and shields the added nuclear charge fairly well. Neighbouring transition metals are therefore near-interchangeable in a lattice, and they form alloys freely.

The other three options are simply false of transition metals as a group: their electronic configurations, enthalpies of atomisation and oxidation states all differ from one element to the next.

rows.stem:
Consider the following reaction :
Methylcyclobutane \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2},\ \text{UV light}}\) ?
The major product obtained is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the reactant AND all four options are printed as drawn ring structures rather than as formulae. On the page: the reactant is a plain four-sided ring (a rectangle, no inner bonds) with a bond from its top-right corner to CH3, then an arrow labelled Br2, UV light. Option (A) is the same ring with CH3 off one corner and Br off the corner directly below it; (B) has CH3 and Br off the SAME corner; (C) has CH2Br off one corner; (D) has CH3 off one corner and Br off the diagonally opposite corner. The names above record the substituent identities and positions faithfully but cannot show that the ring is drawn square rather than hexagonal, which is the fact a reader most needs to check - attach the real crop. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The major product is 1-BROMO-1-METHYLCYCLOBUTANE.

Bromine under ULTRAVIOLET LIGHT reacts by free radicals, and a bromine radical abstracts the hydrogen that leaves behind the MOST STABLE radical.

Of the hydrogens available, the one on the ring carbon that also carries the methyl group is the only TERTIARY hydrogen — that carbon is attached to three other carbons. Removing it leaves a tertiary radical, stabilised by electron release from three alkyl groups, and the bromine then attaches there.

The other options come from abstracting a less favourable hydrogen: a secondary ring hydrogen gives the 2- or 3-substituted product, and a hydrogen from the methyl group itself would be PRIMARY, the least favourable of all.

The order of radical stability — tertiary above secondary above primary — is the whole content of the question.

rows.stem: Which one of the following compounds has the highest \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) value ?
rows.solution:
The HIGHEST \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) — meaning the WEAKEST acid — belongs to p-CRESOL.

Acidity is decided by what the substituent does to the PHENOXIDE ion left behind. Electron-WITHDRAWING groups disperse its negative charge, stabilise it and strengthen the acid; electron-RELEASING groups concentrate the charge and weaken it.

The methyl group of p-cresol is electron RELEASING, so it is the only one of the four that makes the acid weaker than phenol itself — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 10.2 against phenol's 10.

All three others carry nitro groups and are stronger. m-Nitrophenol at about 8.4 gets only the inductive pull, since a meta group cannot reach the charge by resonance. p-Nitrophenol at about 7.1 gets both. And picric acid, with three nitro groups, is about 0.4 — the strongest of the four by a very wide margin.

Anisole with hydrogen iodide gives PHENOL AND IODOMETHANE.

Cleaving an ether with hydrogen iodide always breaks the bond on the side that can accept the iodide, and here one side is an ARYL group. An aryl-oxygen bond has partial double bond character from resonance with the ring — the oxygen's lone pair is fed into the ring, shortening and strengthening the bond — so it will not break.

The iodide therefore attacks the METHYL carbon instead:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}OCH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_3I}\)

The option giving iodobenzene and methanol is the trap: it breaks exactly the bond that cannot break. The other two insert a hydroxyl or an iodine where neither belongs.

rows.stem: Which of the following compounds on treatment with benzene sulphonyl choride forms product insoluble in alkali ?
rows.solution:
The compound is DIMETHYLAMINE, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH}\).

Benzenesulphonyl chloride is Hinsberg's reagent, and the test turns on how many hydrogens remain on the nitrogen after it reacts.

A SECONDARY amine gives a sulphonamide with NO hydrogen left on its nitrogen — both positions are now taken, one by each methyl group and one by the sulphonyl group. With no acidic hydrogen there is nothing for alkali to remove, so the product is INSOLUBLE in alkali, which is what the question describes.

A PRIMARY amine would leave one hydrogen on the nitrogen, made acidic by the two electron-withdrawing oxygens beside it, so its product DISSOLVES in alkali — that rules out both ethylamine and aniline. A TERTIARY amine has no nitrogen-hydrogen bond at all and does not react in the first place, so trimethylamine gives no product to test.

rows.stem: Which of the following amines gives carbylamine reaction ?
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — option (D) alone is printed as a drawn structure: a hexagonal ring bearing three inner double bonds (a Kekule benzene ring) joined to -NH-CH3. It is named losslessly above as C6H5-NH-CH3, so the row is fully answerable from text; the drawing is worth showing because it is the paper's own way of setting this option apart from the three condensed formulae beside it. Options (A), (B) and (C) are printed as ordinary condensed formulae. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
ETHYLAMINE, \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\), gives the carbylamine reaction.

The test detects PRIMARY amines ONLY. Chloroform with alcoholic potassium hydroxide generates dichlorocarbene, and forming an isocyanide requires the nitrogen to give up BOTH of its hydrogens to that carbon:
\(\mathrm{R{-}NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R{-}NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The foul smell of the isocyanide is the test's signature.

A SECONDARY amine has only ONE hydrogen on its nitrogen where two are needed, so diethylamine and N-methylaniline both fail. A TERTIARY amine has none at all, so triethylamine cannot even begin.

The test works for primary AROMATIC amines too — aniline gives it — so it is the number of nitrogen-hydrogen bonds, not the kind of carbon skeleton, that decides.

rows.stem: ‘Night-Blindness’ is caused by the deficiency of Vitamin :
rows.solution:
Night-blindness is caused by a deficiency of VITAMIN A.

Vitamin A is needed to make rhodopsin, the pigment in the retina that responds to dim light. Without it the eye adapts poorly to darkness, and prolonged deficiency goes on to dry the cornea — xerophthalmia — and can end in blindness.

It is FAT SOLUBLE, so the body can store a reserve in the liver, which is why the deficiency develops slowly.

Of the others: a deficiency of the B group gives beri-beri or cheilosis depending on which member is short, vitamin C deficiency gives scurvy, and vitamin K deficiency gives increased clotting time.

rows.stem: When the initial concentration of a reactant is doubled in the reaction, the half life period remains same. The order of reaction is :
rows.solution:
The order is FIRST.

A half-life that does not change when the starting concentration is doubled is the SIGNATURE of first order. Its expression
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{k}\)
contains no concentration term at all, so the time to fall by half is the same whatever concentration the reaction starts from.

Every other order behaves differently. For ZERO order \(t_{1/2} = [\mathrm{A}]_0/2k\), directly proportional to the starting concentration, so doubling it doubles the half-life. For SECOND order \(t_{1/2} = 1/k[\mathrm{A}]_0\), inversely proportional, so doubling it HALVES the half-life.

That is why radioactive decay, which is first order, can be quoted as a single half-life for the isotope with no mention of how much is present.

rows.stem: Which of the following is a secondary cell ?
rows.solution:
The LEAD STORAGE CELL is the secondary cell.

A SECONDARY cell is one whose reaction can be driven backwards — applying an external voltage greater than the cell's own reverses the electrode reactions and restores the original reactants, so the cell can be recharged and used again many times. In the lead storage battery both electrodes become coated with lead sulphate on discharge, and charging converts that back to lead and lead dioxide.

The dry cell and the mercury cell are PRIMARY cells: their reactions are effectively irreversible, and once the reactants sealed inside are used up the cell is discarded.

The DANIELL cell is the interesting distractor. It is a galvanic cell, the textbook example of one — but it is not designed for recharging, and it is classified as a primary cell.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}\mathrm{H}\) and \(\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}\mathrm{V}\) are zero for non-ideal solutions.
Reason (R) : Solute-solvent interactions are not same as pure solute-solute and pure solvent-solvent interactions in non-ideal solutions.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

\(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H\) and \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}V\) are zero for IDEAL solutions, not for non-ideal ones. Indeed being zero is part of what DEFINES an ideal solution, along with obedience to Raoult's law over the whole range of composition. The Assertion attaches the property to exactly the wrong class.

The Reason is correct, and it is precisely why the Assertion fails. Heat is absorbed or released on mixing only when the new solute-solvent interactions differ in strength from the solute-solute and solvent-solvent interactions broken to make room for them. In a NON-ideal solution they do differ — that is what makes it non-ideal — so the energy does not balance and neither quantity is zero.

Where the interactions are all alike, as in benzene with toluene, both quantities vanish and the solution is ideal.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Rate of reaction increases with increase in temperature.
Reason (R) : Number of effective collisions increase with increase in temperature.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Raising the temperature does increase the rate of a reaction — near room temperature a rise of ten degrees roughly doubles or trebles it, which is a far larger effect than the modest increase in collision frequency alone could produce.

The Reason names the right mechanism. What matters is not the number of collisions but the number of EFFECTIVE ones — collisions carrying at least the activation energy and occurring in the right orientation. The fraction of molecules with that much energy is \(e^{-E_a/RT}\), and it climbs steeply with temperature.

Doubling the rate for a ten-degree rise takes only a small shift in the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, because the molecules concerned are in its high-energy tail, where a small change in temperature moves the population a great deal.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The boiling point of ethanol is higher than that of dimethyl ether.
Reason (R) : Dimethyl ether molecules are associated through hydrogen bonding.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Ethanol does boil higher than dimethyl ether — 351 K against 248 K — although the two are isomers with the same formula and the same mass.

But the Reason attributes the hydrogen bonding to the wrong compound. DIMETHYL ETHER molecules are NOT associated through hydrogen bonding: neither of its hydrogens sits on an electronegative atom, both being on carbon, so its molecules can only manage weak dipole-dipole attraction.

It is ETHANOL whose molecules associate, its hydrogen sitting on OXYGEN. Corrected in that direction, the Reason would have explained the Assertion exactly; as written it names the opposite molecule, and if it were true it would predict the opposite boiling points.

The ether's oxygen can still ACCEPT a hydrogen bond, which is why dimethyl ether dissolves in water; what it cannot do is DONATE one.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Aniline undergoes Friedel-Crafts reaction.
Reason (R) : Aniline forms salt with \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\), the Lewis acid in Friedel-Crafts reaction.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

Aniline does NOT undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction — the Assertion claims the opposite and is therefore false.

The Reason is correct and states exactly why. Aluminium chloride is a LEWIS ACID, and the nitrogen's lone pair is exactly what it seeks, so the catalyst bonds to the nitrogen and forms a salt. Two things then go wrong at once: the catalyst is tied up and unavailable to generate the electrophile, and the nitrogen now carries a POSITIVE charge, which makes it strongly deactivating and meta directing rather than the powerful activator it was.

So the Reason gives the ground on which the Assertion fails. Acetylating the amino group first solves the problem, which is how an aniline is acylated in practice.

rows.stem:
Write the reactions of glucose with :
(a) \(\mathrm{H_2N-OH}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) water
rows.solution:
(a) WITH HYDROXYLAMINE, D-glucose gives its OXIME. The nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon, water is lost, and a carbon-nitrogen double bond forms:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{H_2N{-}OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH({=}N{-}OH)(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is glucose oxime. That an ammonia derivative condenses with it at all is one of the proofs that glucose contains a CARBONYL group.

(b) WITH BROMINE WATER, glucose is oxidised to a six carbon carboxylic acid, GLUCONIC ACID:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2}\text{ water}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)

Bromine water is a MILD oxidising agent, too mild to attack a hydroxyl group, so the only thing in the molecule it can have oxidised is the ALDEHYDE — which is how the aldehyde group specifically is established. Concentrated nitric acid, being stronger, oxidises BOTH ends and gives the dicarboxylic saccharic acid instead.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
Complete and balance the following chemical equations :
(a) \(\mathrm{KMnO_4} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{2MnO_4^{-} + 5C_2O_4^{2-} + 16H^{+} \longrightarrow}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Heating potassium permanganate decomposes it, manganese ending in two different oxidation states — \(+6\) in the manganate and \(+4\) in the dioxide — with oxygen released:
\(2\mathrm{KMnO_4} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}\)

Check the balance: potassium 2 both sides, manganese 2 both sides, oxygen 8 on the left against \(4 + 2 + 2 = 8\) on the right.

(b) Permanganate oxidises oxalate to carbon dioxide in acid, manganese falling from \(+7\) to \(+2\):
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 5\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}} + 16\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 10\mathrm{CO_2} + 8\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Ten electrons change hands: two permanganates take five each, and five oxalates give up two each as carbon rises from \(+3\) to \(+4\). Note that each oxalate yields TWO molecules of carbon dioxide, which is where the 10 comes from.

This reaction is the basis of the volumetric estimation of oxalic acid, and it is autocatalytic — the \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) produced speeds it up, which is why the first drop of permanganate decolourises slowly and the rest quickly.

rows.stem:
(a) Which halogen compound in the following pair will react faster in \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction and why ?
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(Br)-CH_3}\)   or   \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(CH_3)_2-Br}\)
(b) Why is the dipole moment of chlorobenzene lower than that of cyclohexyl chloride ?
rows.solution:
(a) 2-BROMO-2-METHYLPROPANE, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}Br}\), reacts faster.

The rate of an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction is set entirely by how easily the CARBOCATION forms, since that is the slow step — so the question is which cation is the more stable.

This compound is TERTIARY, and the cation it gives is stabilised by electron release from THREE methyl groups. 2-Bromopropane is SECONDARY and gives a cation with only two.

Note that the same bulk which favours \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) HINDERS \(\mathrm{S_N}2\), where the nucleophile must reach the carbon from behind — which is why the two orders run exactly opposite to each other.

(b) Because the carbon holding the chlorine is \(sp^2\) HYBRIDISED in chlorobenzene and \(sp^3\) in cyclohexyl chloride.

Two consequences follow, and both reduce the dipole. An \(sp^2\) carbon has more s character, so it is MORE ELECTRONEGATIVE and pulls the shared pair back towards itself, leaving the bond less polar than it would otherwise be. And the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond is SHORTER, partly from that hybridisation and partly from resonance, which gives it some double bond character — and dipole moment is charge times distance, so a shorter bond means a smaller moment.

Measured: about 1.69 D for chlorobenzene against 2.15 D for cyclohexyl chloride.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the reactions involved in the following :
(i) Reimer-Tiemann reaction
(ii) Kolbe's reaction
(b) Name the reagent used in the bromination of phenol to form 2,4,6-Tribromophenol.
rows.solution:
(a)(i) REIMER-TIEMANN REACTION. Chloroform with aqueous alkali generates DICHLOROCARBENE, which attacks the phenoxide ion at its ORTHO position; acidification then frees the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{CHCl_3} + \text{aq. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO}\)
The product is salicylaldehyde. The alkali is needed twice over — to make the carbene and to convert phenol into the more strongly activated phenoxide ion.

(ii) KOLBE'S REACTION. Phenol is first converted to sodium phenoxide, which attacks CARBON DIOXIDE at its ortho position; acidification then frees the acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5O^-Na^+} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{CO_2}} \mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH}\)
The product is salicylic acid — the starting material for aspirin.

The two reactions are the same idea with different electrophiles: phenoxide is nucleophilic enough to attack even a feeble electrophile, and both attacks go ORTHO.

(b) The reagent is BROMINE WATER — bromine in aqueous solution.

Water is what makes all three positions substitute at once. It lets the phenol ionise to phenoxide, which is even more strongly activating than phenol itself, so no catalyst is needed and the white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol appears immediately.

Bromine in a NON-polar solvent such as carbon disulphide, at low temperature, stops after ONE substitution and gives a mixture of the ortho and para isomers — same reagent, different medium, different product.
